questions.stem: A 74-year-old man presented with 2 days of watery diarrhea and 1 day of large fluid-filled skin lesions. He had a history of cirrhotic liver disease. He had recently returned from a fishing trip on the US Gulf Coast. He had been swimming in the hotel pool but not the sea. On examination he was dehydrated, his temperature was 38.3°C, blood pressure 88/52mmHg, heart rate 115 beats/minute. Investigations: Blood cultures: curved gram-negative rods seen on microscopy
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely infective cause?
questions.explanation: Vibrio vulnificus This patient has acquired systemic Vibrio vulnificus infection following the ingestion of seafood in the US Gulf coast. Patients with cirrhosis or hemochromatosis are particularly susceptible to systemic infection and have a high mortality rate, ranging from 40% to 90%. They can present with fever and hypotension, developing bullous lesions and cellulitis. This patient is bacteremic with Vibrio as evidenced by the curved gram-negative rods indicative of Vibrio vulnificus and other Vibrio spp. Patients with a presumptive diagnosis of V. vulnificus septicemia should be started immediately on antibiotic therapy and managed aggressively in an intensive care unit. A tetracycline plus a third-generation cephalosporin is recommended.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q10

questions.question: Patient with hemochromatosis and ate raw oysters. [image-based question: picture of bullous lower extremity lesions shown]

parts.text: What is the organism?

questions.question: Name the most likely pathogen for the following scenarios.

parts.text: AML patient with central venous catheter with sepsis and haemorrhagic bullous skin lesions. The aspirate is growing a GPR.
Asplenic patient with sepsis after dog bite.
Necrotizing scalp infection after swimming.
CVID patient with chronic abdominal pain and diarrhea.

questions.model_answer: a) AML patient with CVC, sepsis, hemorrhagic bullous lesions, GPR growing on aspirate: most likely Bacillus cereus (or consider Clostridium species) - hemorrhagic bullae in neutropenic host with CVC and gram-positive rod strongly suggests Bacillus cereus bacteremia. b) Asplenic patient with sepsis after dog bite: Capnocytophaga canimorsus. c) Necrotizing scalp infection after swimming: Aeromonas hydrophila (freshwater exposure) - consider Vibrio vulnificus if saltwater exposure. d) CVID patient with chronic abdominal pain/diarrhea: Giardia lamblia.

questions.question: 40yo M, hx IVDU, recently incarcerated seen at OPAT with purulent cellulitis of R leg.

parts.text: What are the most common organisms causing this condition - give 2?

On further questioning he says he was at the beach and cut his foot on a shell before the infection started. You want to cover Vibrio vulnificus but are concerned about compliance. Give an oral antibiotic option for monotherapy to cover the pathogens of concern.
There were adverse effects related to the oral monotherapy you gave - give two regimens (IV +/- PO) that are alternatives. PO can be given max BID, IV max once daily.
Name 5 other organisms that can cause marine associated SSTIs

questions.model_answer:
a) 2 most common organisms causing purulent cellulitis in this context (IVDU): Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA) and Streptococcus pyogenes (group A Streptococcus).
b) Oral monotherapy option covering Vibrio vulnificus: doxycycline (has activity against Vibrio vulnificus as well as reasonable MRSA coverage).
c) 2 alternative regimens (IV +/- PO, PO max BID, IV max once daily): (1) ceftriaxone IV once daily + ciprofloxacin PO BID; (2) cefotaxime IV once daily + levofloxacin PO once daily.
d) 5 other organisms causing marine-associated SSTIs: Aeromonas hydrophila, Mycobacterium marinum, Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae, Vibrio alginolyticus, Vibrio parahaemolyticus (Shewanella algae also acceptable).

questions.question: Purulent cellulitis in homeless individual.

parts.text: Name the two most likely pathogens to cause this
Tells you he cut it in sea water concerning for vibrio vulnificus, what empiric oral agent could cover all 3 organisms?
He gets allergy to that agent, design two regimens with a single daily IV and/or BID oral that could be used instead of above.
Name 5 organisms (genus and species) of acute water SSTI.

questions.model_answer:
a) The two most likely pathogens causing purulent cellulitis in this population: Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA) and Streptococcus pyogenes (group A Streptococcus).
b) Doxycycline is a reasonable single empiric oral agent providing activity against MRSA, streptococci, and Vibrio vulnificus.
c) Two alternative regimens (single daily-dose IV and/or twice-daily oral, maximum two drugs each): Regimen 1 - ceftriaxone 1-2 g IV once daily (covers Streptococcus and Vibrio) plus trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole PO twice daily (covers MRSA). Regimen 2 - ertapenem 1 g IV once daily (covers Streptococcus, Vibrio, and other gram-negatives) plus linezolid PO/IV 600 mg twice daily (covers MRSA and Streptococcus).
d) Five organisms causing acute water-associated skin/soft tissue infection: Vibrio vulnificus, Aeromonas hydrophila, Mycobacterium marinum, Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae, and Edwardsiella tarda.

questions.question: Homeless man comes to OPAT clinic. He has purulent cellulitis.

parts.text: What are the two organisms most likely to be responsible?
He remembers that he cut his leg on a seashell by the seashore. You want to cover for Vibrio vulnificus. What is the best oral regimen to empirically cover these organisms?
Give two further regimens can be IV or oral. If IV can only be given once per day. If po can only be given twice per day. Can only have two drugs max in each regimen.
Name 5 more organisms that can cause “marine associated” skin/soft tissue infection.

questions.model_answer:
a) Two most likely organisms: Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA) and Streptococcus pyogenes (group A Streptococcus).
b) Best oral empiric regimen to also cover Vibrio vulnificus: doxycycline (active against MRSA, streptococci, and Vibrio vulnificus).
c) Two alternative regimens (IV once daily and/or oral twice daily, maximum two drugs each): Regimen 1 - ceftriaxone 1-2 g IV once daily plus trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole PO twice daily. Regimen 2 - ertapenem 1 g IV once daily plus linezolid 600 mg PO/IV twice daily.
d) Five further marine-associated SSTI organisms: Aeromonas hydrophila, Mycobacterium marinum, Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae, Edwardsiella tarda, and Shewanella putrefaciens.

questions.question: You are seeing a gentleman with liver disease who has just been on vacation in Florida eating quite a few raw oysters. He now presents with sepsis.

parts.text: What organism is this?
What are THREE clinical presentations of this organism?
What are FOUR risk factors associated with severe disease in this organism?
What are two viruses you could get from eating oysters?

questions.model_answer:
a) Organism: Vibrio vulnificus.
b) 3 clinical presentations: (1) primary septicemia, (2) wound infection/necrotizing fasciitis, (3) gastroenteritis.
c) 4 risk factors for severe disease: (1) chronic liver disease/cirrhosis, (2) iron overload (hemochromatosis), (3) diabetes mellitus, (4) immunocompromised state (e.g., chronic renal disease or immunosuppressive therapy).
d) 2 viruses from raw oysters: norovirus and hepatitis A virus.

questions.question:
Q57 (2011 PM, 2007)
Alcoholic goes swimming in New Orleans water (salt water) and develops bullous cellulitis. Alternate stem: Cirrhotic man floated for 2 days in seawater around New Orleans, presents with fever and bullous leg lesions. Bacteremia with curved GNB.

parts.text: A) Name 2 possible organisms / What is the organism?

cohort_answer.text: Vibrio vulnificus. Others: Vibrio parahemolyticus, Vibrio alginolyticus. Also Shewanella (can also cause necrotizing infections, but not curved) - oxidase and catalase-positive non-fermenter gram-negative rod producing hydrogen sulfide

questions.question:
Q57 (2011 PM, 2007)
Alcoholic goes swimming in New Orleans water (salt water) and develops bullous cellulitis.

parts.text: B) 2 treatment options? If sepsis +/- necrotizing fasciitis?

cohort_answer.text: Cellulitis without sepsis/nec fasc: Doxy or Cipro. For sepsis/nec fasc: immediate surgical debridement, combination of Ceftriaxone with Doxy or Cipro

questions.question: Q60 (2008). Vacationing woman in the Caribbean with abrasions (coral/shells) and rapidly progressive cellulitis. Not responsive to cephalexin with bullae

parts.text: A) What is the organism?
B) What would you treat her with?

cohort_answer.text: Vibrio vulnificus (exposure to salt water of puncture wounds, incubation 3-7 days). Treatment: mild-moderate - monotherapy with tetracycline or FQ x5-7d; severe or bacteremic - doxy + ceftriaxone or cefotaxime (IDSA); debridement of devitalized tissue or amputation may be lifesaving; FQ/3rd gen ceph/doxy highly active, cipro+cefotaxime synergistic

questions.question: Organisms associated with soft tissue infection following water exposure

parts.text: Name 5 organisms

cohort_answer.text: Fresh water: Aeromonas hydrophilia, Burkholderia pseudomallei, Streptococcus iniae, Chromobacterium violaceum, Edwardsiella tarda, Plesiomonas shigelloides, Pseudomonas. Salt water: Vibrio vulnificus, Mycobacterium marinum (also fresh), Mycobacterium fortuitum (also fresh), Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae, Shewanella spp. Also Prototheca in immunocompromised.

questions.question: Cirrhotic man floated for 2 days in seawater around New Orleans. Presents with fever and bullous leg lesions. Bacteremic with curved GNBs.

parts.text: Name 2 possible organisms
Describe tx

cohort_answer.text: Vibrio vulnificus, Vibrio parahaemolyticus (GI illness predominant), Vibrio alginolyticus (nec fasc reported). Treatment: urgent surgical debridement, 3rd gen ceph + FQ/Doxy (Ceftriaxone 1g IV daily + Doxy 100mg PO BID or Cipro 500mg PO BID)

questions.question: Lady with intermittent rectal bleeding presents with fever hypotension and a spontaneous bullous lesion on her leg. Aspiration is done and shown. [image-based question: gram stain shown]

parts.text: Most likely organism?
What are two characteristic features seen on gram stain illustrated?
What is one condition which is directly associated with acquisition of this infection?
What empiric treatment do you begin?
Other non-abx treatments (2)

cohort_answer.text: Organism: Clostridium septicum. Gram stain features: Gram variable rods; Terminal spore with drumstick appearance. Associated condition: Colonic malignancy. Empiric treatment: Penicillin + Clindamycin. Other treatments: Surgical debridement; Hyperbaric O2 (controversial as C septicum is aerotolerant); Colonoscopy after infection to assess for colon cancer

questions.question: Patient with IVDU develops a skin/soft tissue infection.

parts.text: 2 most likely pathogens.
Now gets Vibrio - 1 drug.
Without using the 1 drug chosen, come up with 2 regimens (IV can only be once daily, and PO can only be twice daily or less frequent)
List 5 marine borne agents associated with skin/soft tissue infections

cohort_answer.text: Pathogens: GAS, S. aureus. Vibrio drug: Ciprofloxacin. Alternative regimens: IV CRO + doxy, or CRO + levofloxacin (can also use ceftazidime as 3rd gen ceph but dosing frequency 3x daily). Marine-borne agents: Vibrio vulnificus, Plesiomonas sp., Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Mycobacterium marinum, Aeromonas hydrophila, Shewanella spp. (family Vibrionaceae), Streptococcus iniae, Burkholderia pseudomallei.

questions.question: 27-year-old with chronic liver disease who has a grand time in Florida and eats some raw oysters. But then he develops sepsis.

parts.text: What is the most likely pathogen (to species level)
Name three different presentations of this pathogen
What are 4 host risk factors for severe disease
Name the 2 most common viruses you can get from oysters

cohort_answer.text: Pathogen: Vibrio vulnificus. Presentations: Wound infections; Gastroenteritis; Primary septicemia. Host risk factors: Alcoholic cirrhosis; Underlying liver disease including cirrhosis and chronic hepatitis; Alcohol use disorder without documented liver disease; Hereditary hemochromatosis; Chronic diseases (DM, RA, CKD, thalassemia major, lymphoma); HIV; Older male. Common viruses from oysters: Norovirus; Sapovirus; Hepatitis A

questions.question: You see a patient with severe sepsis. He recently traveled to Florida where he consumed many raw oysters.

parts.text: What is the most likely bacteria causing his infection?
List THREE clinical syndromes associated with this bacteria.
List THREE risk factors for severe sepsis with this bacteria.
List TWO common viral infections that are associated with eating raw oysters.

questions.model_answer:
a) Most likely bacteria: Vibrio vulnificus.
b) 3 clinical syndromes: (1) primary septicemia (often fulminant bacteremia), (2) wound infection/necrotizing skin and soft tissue infection (from seawater/shellfish exposure), (3) gastroenteritis.
c) 3 risk factors for severe sepsis: (1) chronic liver disease/cirrhosis, (2) iron overload states (e.g., hemochromatosis), (3) immunocompromising conditions (e.g., diabetes mellitus, chronic renal disease, or immunosuppressive therapy).
d) 2 viral infections associated with raw oyster consumption: norovirus and hepatitis A virus.

questions.question: Bonus: Describe type of water exposure, clinical syndrome, and treatment for: Aeromonas, Burkholderia pseudomallei, Vibrio vulnificus, Streptococcus iniae, Mycobacterium marinum, Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae

parts.text: Describe type of water exposure for each
Describe their clinical syndrome
Treatment for each
Prophylactic therapy (assuming wound exposure)

cohort_answer.text: Water type: Aeromonas - fresh water; Burkholderia pseudomallei - fresh water; Vibrio vulnificus - salt water; Streptococcus iniae - fresh water; Mycobacterium marinum - salt or fresh water; Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae - salt water. Clinical: Aeromonas - cellulitis/myonecrosis/rhabdo/ecthyma gangrenosum, men:women 3:1, also leech-associated; Burkholderia pseudomallei - melioidosis, intracellular GNB, skin ulcers/abscesses failing PO abx, worse in cirrhotics; Vibrio vulnificus - rapidly progressive infection, necrotizing infections, hemorrhagic bullae, linked to raw oysters/puncture wounds; Streptococcus iniae - assoc with tilapia fish farming, impetigo/cellulitis; Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae - erysipeloid of Rosenbach, subacute cellulitis of fingers/hands; Mycobacterium marinum - indolent (mean incubation 21d), papules/nodules progressing to ulceration/scar, sporotrichoid spread. Treatment: Aeromonas – Doxycycline + FQ/3rd gen Ceph; Burkholderia pseudomallei – Ceftazidime or carbapenem; Vibrio vulnificus – Doxycycline + 3rd gen ceph; Streptococcus iniae – beta-lactam; Mycobacterium marinum – Clarithromycin + Ethambutol/Rifampin; Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae – penicillin/ampicillin/cephalexin. Prophylaxis: no clear guideline; reasonable for deep puncture/laceration, wounds needing surgical repair, wounds with water exposure outside treated pools, crush injury, vascular/lymphatic compromise, hands/feet/face/genital area, near bone/joint, immunocompromised/diabetic/liver disease. Empiric: 1st gen cephalosporin OR clindamycin + fluoroquinolone; salt water add doxycycline; soil/sewage add metronidazole; wash wound, debride, tetanus prophylaxis
